Huiwon, from a flash to a spark

There’s a white flower in “light” and a crawling insect in the release note for “Birth…”. Two records trace what changes in Huiwon’s writing and who plays the parts.

BY indiek / 2026-11-23

A white flower appears near the end of “light,” the closing track on Huiwon’s 2025 EP 反骨商會 (반골상회). By then the speaker has spent much of the song asking for something to stay. The Korean title, 섬광, means a flash, which gives the plea a particular urgency. A flash is over in an instant. A flower needs time. [1] [2]

An insect crawls along the ground in the release note for Huiwon’s July 2026 single “Birth…,” where it’s an image of stirring into life again. Read together, the songs give light and fire different jobs. A flash carries a wish for something to stay. In the later song, the speaker wants a spark to travel. [2] [3] [4]

A heartbeat heard, stopped, heard again

The plea against disappearing sits beside a more unsettling reversal. The speaker wants someone to hear their heartbeat, then asks for it to be stopped. The request to hear it returns at the end, alongside the wish to let the flower bloom. Those final requests leave the earlier contradiction in place. [2]

Writing in Korean Indie, Chris P describes a minimally accompanied vocal opening into a fuller rock arrangement. On the recording, Huiwon (천희원) is credited with arrangement, MIDI programming and bass, and shares the guitar credit with Jo Yu-ik (조유익). Yeo Jin-woo (여진우) played drums. [1] [6]

Four songs, different rooms

POCLANOS introduces 反骨商會 as band-based music with the defiance of being eighteen. Even the release note’s image of bones growing backwards gives that defiance a physical shape. Across the four songs, Huiwon wrote the lyrics and music, while the recordings draw on different arrangements and players. The lyrics shift just as sharply, moving from fond details of an ordinary day to a speaker who wants out of their own skin. [1] [8] [9]

The opener, “2008,” keeps circling back to somewhere familiar. The lyric remembers a strange sky and a smile against slightly dirty wallpaper. It also imagines lifting a telephone receiver to bring back a voice. What makes the song’s nostalgia specific is how ordinary those details are. [8]

On “soultrap.exe,” the person looking out has trouble seeing clearly. Their gaze is compared to a low-resolution camera, and their body becomes somewhere they want to get out of. Even the title ends in a file extension. Where “2008” pieces together a place the speaker keeps returning to, “soultrap.exe” gives the speaker a close-up they would rather escape. [8] [9]

On “2008,” Lee Seo-hyeong played bass and Yeo Jin-woo played drums. On “soultrap.exe,” Huiwon is credited with both, along with keys and MIDI. Heo Se-gwa (허세과) arranged “Found and Lost” and is credited with guitar, bass and MIDI programming. Huiwon wrote all three songs, with different players shaping each recording. [1]

“Found and Lost,” just before “light” on the EP, gives the later single a point of comparison. Its speaker wants to reach a place and insists on continuing even at the risk of burning. In “Birth…,” the speaker asks for the embers to spread. What was a risk of pressing on in the earlier song becomes part of how the later one imagines getting underway. [1] [5] [4]

“2008” and “light” live

Huiwon posted live clips of “2008” and “light,” the first and last songs on the EP, on the artist’s own YouTube channel. Both performances are in the listening list above. [1] [10] [11]

What “Birth…” is ready for

The Korean title 태동 means movement in the womb and can also mean the first stirrings of something new. In the song, the speaker imagines being woken even if it hurts. Huiwon wrote and arranged the track. Song Ju-won (송주원) played guitar and Shin Ji-min (신지민) played drums. The bassist Lee Seo-hyeong (이서형) also played on “2008,” the EP’s opener. [7] [4] [3] [1]

The insect in the release note stays close to the ground. In the lyric, the speaker wants embers to spread. The two images sit at different scales, a first movement and a wish for it to carry farther. The ellipsis in both the Korean and English titles suits a song still occupied with getting underway. [3] [4]

The refrain of “Birth…” asks for speed and for regret to wait. There’s a difference between getting past regret and asking for a little more time before dealing with it. The song makes room for the second possibility. Its speaker can imagine moving before they’re ready to look back. [4]
